overview: This file consists of a March 18, 1943 despatch from the American Embassy in Kuibyshev transmitting a British-supplied English translation of E. Pigulevskaya’s Soviet journal article, “Ferrous Metallurgy in Japan Under War Conditions,” published in November–December 1942. The article surveys Japan’s wartime supplies and productive capacity in iron ore, pig iron, steel, scrap metal, coking coal, and metallurgical coke across Japan, Korea, Manchuria, occupied China, Malaya, the Philippines, and other Southeast Asian territories. Using production estimates, Japanese press reports, and descriptions of individual mines, plants, railways, and ports, it argues that blockade, shipping vulnerability, damaged infrastructure, shortages of capital and skilled labor, and partisan warfare prevented the Japanese empire from securing enough raw materials for a prolonged mechanized war.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 270 transmitting a Soviet article on Japanese metallurgy
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, for the Ambassador, American Embassy, Kuibyshev
subfiles.about: The American Embassy transmits copies of a British-supplied translation of a Soviet analysis of Japan’s wartime ferrous-metals industry.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reports that the Commercial Secretariat of the British Embassy in Kuibyshev supplied an English translation of an article from the November–December 1942 issue of Mirovoe Khozyaistvo i Mirovaya Politika. The Embassy reproduced the translation for the State Department and sent a copy to Moscow.

subfiles.title: Translation of E. Pigulevskaya, “Ferrous Metallurgy in Japan Under War Conditions”
subfiles.about: A Soviet writer assesses the productive capacity, raw-material base, and wartime vulnerabilities of the Japanese empire’s iron and steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Pigulevskaya argues that Japan entered the Pacific War with accumulated metal reserves but remained heavily dependent on imported iron ore, scrap, pig iron, and coking coal. The article compares industrial capacity and actual production in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria and then surveys mines, plants, coalfields, railways, and ports throughout occupied China, Malaya, the Philippines, French Indochina, and the Netherlands East Indies. It emphasizes the effects of blockade, destroyed equipment, inadequate transportation, shortages of capital and skilled labor, and partisan warfare on Japanese efforts to exploit conquered resources. It concludes that scrap-collection campaigns and imperial expansion could provide only temporary relief and that Japan’s comparatively weak metallurgical base was inadequate for a long, large-scale mechanized war.

interest: The file preserves a detailed Soviet wartime assessment of Japanese industrial weakness as it circulated through British and American diplomatic channels in Kuibyshev. Its mine-by-mine and plant-by-plant discussion, production estimates, citations to Japanese newspapers, and attention to transport routes make it useful for studying Allied economic intelligence, Japan’s imperial resource system, and contemporary expectations about the sustainability of its war economy. It is also valuable as evidence of Soviet analytical and propagandistic framing, although its estimates, polemical conclusions, and heavily transliterated place names require comparison with Japanese and other Allied sources.
